The high temperature tensile properties of a Cu–4.5Ti alloy have been investigated in the temperature range from room temperature (RT) to 550 ◦C in solution treated (ST) and peak-aged (PA) conditions.

evidence.quote: Microstructure of the alloy at room temperature is shown in Fig. 6(a) for comparison [7], which depicts equiaxed grains with annealing twins.
Yield strength of solution treated alloy was found to be constant at 450 ± 10 MPa from room temperature (RT) up to 350 °C
increased to a maximum of 520 MPa at 450 ◦C
decreased to 470 MPa at the test temperature of 550 ◦C
variation of YS with test temperature was observed to be constant at 680 ± 10 MPa up to 350 °C
reached a final value of 450 MPa at 550 ◦C
It was constant at 680 ± 10 MPa up to 350 °C
increased to 730 MPa at 450 ◦C
decreased to 560 MPa at 550 ◦C
constant at 890 ± 10 MPa up to 350 ◦C and decreased thereafter, to a value of 530 MPa at 550 ◦C
decreased thereafter, to a value of 530 MPa at 550 ◦C
elongation decreased marginally with increasing temperature, from 29% at room temperature to 27% at the test temperature of 350 ◦C
from 29% at room temperature to 27% at the test temperature of 350 ◦C
continued up to the test temperature of 550 ◦C reaching a value of 6%
It decreased from 20% at room temperature to 18% at 350 ◦C
It decreased from 20% at room temperature to 18% at 350 ◦C
continuously with test temperature up to 550 ◦C to a value of 7%
n is found to be constant at 0.21 ± 0.01 from RT to 350 ◦C
ended up with a value of 0.08 at the test temperature of 450 ◦C
The n of peak-aged alloy showed constancy from RT to 350 ◦C at a value of 0.11 ± 0.01
reaching a value of 0.08 at the test temperature of 450 ◦C
In situ age hardening during testing at 450 ◦C resulting in the precipitation of ordered, metastable and coherent Cu4Ti, β′ phase is attributed to the increase in strength.
The decrease in strengths beyond 350 ◦C in the peak-aged alloy is attributed to the coarsening of β′ precipitate particles
Precipitation of equilibrium phase β at the test temperature of 550 ◦C also contributes to decrease in the strength due to over-aging
as the test temperature increases, thermally activated cross-slip dominates which would make the movement of dislocations easy leading to continuous downfall of the strength.
